query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent, slow-growing protective oxide layer forms and persists above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than cracking or spalling? Earlier work investigated CrFeCoNiX and CrMoTiAlY (Y = Ta, Nb, or W) alloy systems and reported that some compositions developed unstable surface oxides prone to cracking and spallation, while the underlying physical causes remain unresolved. Given the requirement for an environmentally stable, chemically inert barrier and prolonged structural integrity, specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted observations, the relevant composition, material-state, exposure, and service boundaries, the prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (where X is Si, Mn, or Al), the selective oxidation of the reactive element governs the formation and stability of the protective oxide. Specifically, alloys with higher Al or Si content form a coherent, slow-growing Al2O3 or SiO2-rich oxide layer that adheres well to the substrate by minimizing lattice and thermal stresses, while alloys with Mn tend to form less coherent, mixed Mn-oxide scales that crack or spall above 900 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys in single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution states
generation.intervention: Expose the alloys to an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere at temperatures above 900 °C
generation.conditions: High-temperature exposure (e.g., 950 °C) in controlled oxidative or corrosive environments that simulate high-temperature service conditions
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a dense, coherent oxide sublayer (Al2O3 or SiO2) that minimizes lattice mismatch with the underlying alloy, thereby reducing stress buildup at the interface
generation.mechanism: Reactive elements (Al or Si) preferentially oxidize to form a continuous, adherent and slow-growing protective oxide layer that acts as a diffusion barrier against further oxidation. In contrast, Mn oxidizes to form less protective, non-coherent oxide phases that cannot accommodate thermal and mechanical stresses, leading to cracking and spallation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys enriched in Al or Si will develop a stable, continuous, slow-growing protective oxide layer with reduced spallation, whereas alloys containing Mn will exhibit rapid oxide growth with evident cracking or spallation under the same conditions.
generation.baseline: Reference behavior is defined by similar alloys with lower levels or absence of the reactive elements (Al or Si), where the oxide layer is less coherent and more prone to failure.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to high-entropy alloys operating above 900 °C in oxidative or corrosive atmospheres; behavior at lower temperatures or non-oxidative conditions may differ.
generation.uncertainty: The influence of the underlying multiphase microstructural transitions on the long-term adhesion and stress accommodation of the oxide layer remains uncertain, as do potential synergistic or antagonistic effects among alloying elements.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate a series of CrFeCoNiX alloys with controlled variations in the reactive element (X = Al, Si, or Mn) and consistent single- or multiphase microstructures. Expose each alloy to a controlled oxidative/corrosive environment at 950 °C for extended durations. Use electron microscopy, X-ray diffraction, and surface spectroscopy to characterize the oxide layer's continuity, phase composition, thickness, and adhesion.
measurements: Phase composition of the oxide and the interface (e.g., presence of Al2O3, SiO2, or Mn-oxide phases)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If alloys enriched in Al or Si do not consistently develop a coherent, adherent protective oxide layer—or if Mn-containing alloys unexpectedly form a protective, stable oxide similar to the Al/Si variants—the proposed mechanism is falsified.

## Abstract
AbstractAs protective coatings for the thermal parts of aero-engines, AlCoCrFeNi coatings have good application prospects. In this study, atmospheric plasma spraying (APS) was used to prepare AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy coatings (HECs), which were oxidized from 650 °C to 1000 °C. The mechanism of the oxide layer formation and the internal phase transition were systematically investigated. The results show that a mixed oxide scale with a laminated structure was formed at the initial stage of oxidation. The redistribution of elements and phase transition occurred in the HECs’ matrix; the BCC/B2 structure transformed to Al-Ni ordered B2 phase and Fe-Cr disordered A2 phase.Keywords: plasma spraying, oxidation behavior, high-entropy coatings, phase transition

## Abstract
Complex multi-element alloys are gaining prominence for structural applications, supplementing steels, and superalloys. Understanding the impact of each element on alloy surfaces due to oxidation is vital in maintaining material integrity. This study investigates oxidation mechanisms in these alloys using a model five-element equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn alloy, in a controlled oxygen environment. The oxidation-induced surface changes correlate with each element’s interactive tendencies with the environment, guided by thermodynamics. Initial oxidation stages follow atomic size and redox potential, with the latter becoming dominant over time, causing composition inversion. The study employs in-situ atom probe tomography, transmission electron microscopy, and X-ray absorption near-edge structure techniques to elucidate the oxidation process and surface oxide structure evolution. Our findings deconvolute the mechanism for compositional and structural changes in the oxide film and will pave the way for a predictive design of complex alloys with improved resistance to oxidation under extreme conditions.
